https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4547.text: Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár (SMER-SD) says the legacy of the First World War remains a powerful reminder that lasting peace can only be achieved through diplomacy. Marking the 112th anniversary of the outbreak of the war on Tuesday, Blanár warned that the failure of diplomacy in 1914 had devastating consequences. He noted that fighting on the Carpathian Front was among the bloodiest of the conflict, with around 400,000 men mobilised from what is now Slovakia and tens of thousands never returning. Blanár also said the world is facing the highest number of armed conflicts since the end of the Second World War, making dialogue and respect for international law more important than ever. He stressed that diplomacy must always be the first choice, not the last resort. The First World War began on 28 July 1914, when Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. The conflict lasted more than four years and claimed the lives of around 10 million soldiers, while millions more were left with lasting physical or psychological injuries. The war also affected present-day Slovakia, where the Carpathian Front stretched from Bardejov to Snina in the country's east. Source: TASR

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-cyber.text: BRUSSELS — The European Union's cybersecurity agency and in-house research center have each begun experimenting with open artificial intelligence models from China, three EU officials have told POLITICO. The Joint Research Centre (JRC) — the EU’s in-house scientific research center — is evaluating “publicly available open-weight models” originating from China, European Commission spokesperson Maciej Berestecki confirmed. The head of ENISA, the bloc's agency responsible for cybersecurity, also said in an interview that his team was now testing Chinese AI. The experiments with Chinese models at the JRC are part of a broader research project to evaluate artificial intelligence that also includes leading models from the United States and Europe, Berestecki said. “Models from different origins are included in a comparative scientific evaluation of their capabilities, performance, limitations and risks,” he said, adding that the JRC is also looking into their potential scientific applications. Advertisement Advertisement AI safety and security — topics currently under intense scrutiny following a series of incidents in which advanced AI models hacked real-world networks during testing activities — are not the core focus of the JRC’s testing activities, according to a different Commission official, who was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive material. Open-weight models are those whose core components are publicly released, allowing anyone to run the model and study how it works. China’s approach to AI has leaned more towards open models than the United States. Some major U.S. tech and AI companies, including chips giant NVIDIA, are investing in open-weight models. Forced to choose The U.S. and China are locked in a race to dominate in the technology, with Europe largely sitting on the sidelines. Without a viable European frontier model, European private and public organizations may be left to choose between American and Chinese providers for advanced AI applications. In a recent speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested Europe should not try to win the frontier AI race. A top German tech company told POLITICO this week it was dropping Europe's leading AI lab Mistral in favor of open-source Chinese models. The JRC has not entered into any “bespoke access” or licensing negotiations with the relevant Chinese developers, Berestecki said. The models are run on the center’s “secure, on-premises scientific infrastructure” and the Commission is not intending to use Chinese models for its own purposes, he added. EU cyber agency ENISA — which has gained access to advanced models from top U.S. AI firms Anthropic, OpenAI and Google — is also experimenting with “a couple” of open-weight Chinese models, its executive director Juhan Lepassaar confirmed in an interview on Wednesday. JRC and ENISA have been tasked with working together to set up an AI testing platform under a recent EU action plan on AI and cyber, the European Commission's attempt to respond to the growing concerns after a series of incidents involving AI systems breaking out of testing environments and breaking into other organizations' digital systems. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, DC, on September 29, 2026. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images) The Brief A new $20 million ad campaign promoting President Donald Trump’s administration is drawing criticism from both parties. The ads are being paid for with money from Trump’s "One Big Beautiful Bill" that was supposed to fund homeland security, according to top Senate Democrats. Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune said it "shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars." Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are calling out the Trump administration over a series of taxpayer-funded ads that experts say could violate a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for propaganda. The three ads started running last week on network and cable TV, as well as streaming platforms. New Trump ads mirror 2024 campaign ads Big picture view: The first 30-second ad features clips of President Donald Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the "largest tax cuts in history," "reigniting American manufacturing" and a call to "defend law and order and police." A second minute-long ad that began airing Friday features scenic videos of Mount Rushmore at night with quotes and clips from Trump’s Fourth of July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary. MORE: Trump says he's sending $500 checks to 1 million Americans: Here's why Over the weekend, a third ad promoting the president resembles a black-and-white video from his own 2024 campaign that shows Trump walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a "final battle" against "globalists" and "warmongers." It ends with Trump staring straight into the camera lens with the "Paid for by the U.S. Government" message printed. What they're saying: In a letter sent to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Sen. Patty Murry of Washington and Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut said that the ads are being paid for with money from Trump’s "One Big Beautiful Bill" that was supposed to fund homeland security. How much did the ads cost? By the numbers: House Democrats said Trump’s director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, moved $20 million from Homeland Security resources to the ad campaign on Sept. 19. MORE: Trump administration rescinds nearly $1B in funds already approved by Congress The next day, a $20 million contract for a "National Media Campaign" was awarded to the Maryland-based LMD Agency, Inc. According to data from AdImpact, more than $2.5 million has been spent on three ads over the past seven days, though that amount could be significantly more. Are the ads legal? Dig deeper: Experts have told The Associated Press that the ads could violate a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for propaganda, though the Government Accountability Office has said propaganda means the government concealed its role in the ad. The Trump ads explicitly state that they’re paid for with taxpayer dollars, according to Axios . "We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," the senators wrote. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, has compared Trump’s ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said it "shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars." The White House has defended the ads, describing them as public service announcements and comparing them to the Biden administration running ads about COVID-19 vaccinations. Experts say these differ from other PSAs because they aren’t designed to help Americans access any specific program. The backstory: Axios reports that previous administrations have also come under scrutiny for ad campaigns. The GAO said the Bush administration’s Medicare news campaign and an EPA campaign under the Obama administration both failed to disclose that the government made the ads.
